title: Seasons in the journal
hook: late in life he tracked when each plant flowered, records some scientists still use

segments.voice: Yesterday, one line a day: the journal Thoreau began because a friend asked. What was your line last night? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

Near the end of Walden, in the chapter on spring, Thoreau does something a poet usually wouldn't. He stops and lists dates. Not dates of his own life, but the days the ice on Walden Pond broke up, year after year, so he could compare. It sits there in the middle of a rapturous chapter about thawing sand and returning birds: a little column of records. The same man who wrote about sucking out the marrow of life also wanted to know, exactly, when the pond let go of winter.
screen: `A LIST IN THE SPRING CHAPTER.` → `WHEN THE ICE BROKE UP.` → `POET AND RECORD-KEEPER.`

segments.voice: First, the habit in Walden. He wrote, "I have travelled a good deal in Concord." It's half a joke. Concord was his home town. He traveled deep instead of far, and part of traveling deep was writing down when things happened: the ice, the first birds, the frogs. Second, the habit grows. In his later journal the noting turns into lists and tables: when this plant leafed out, when that one flowered, when a bird first sang, season after season in the same fields. The poet's eye becomes a careful observer's eye, and he doesn't seem to think of those as enemies. Third, the long reach of a notebook. His records have found readers he couldn't have pictured. Some people who study the seasons have gone back to them to compare flowering times then and now. A man noting a violet in a field near Concord left something useful to strangers far ahead of him. Fourth, records as a spiritual practice. Keeping a record sounds dry. But to know when the maple turns, you have to look at the maple every day. Records are attention that has been kept, not thrown away. They turn a vague feeling, spring seems early this year, into something you can actually see. And they tie you to one place and its slow turning. You start to belong to a particular patch of ground by knowing its calendar.
screen: `TRAVELED A GOOD DEAL IN CONCORD.` · `NOTES TURN INTO TABLES.` · `USEFUL TO STRANGERS LATER.` · then, large: `ATTENTION THAT IS KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note one plant's stage. Pick one plant you'll see again, a tree on your street, a weed by the door, a houseplant. Bring it to mind now, or look at it if it's near. Is it in bud, in leaf, in flower, in fruit, bare? What color is it at the edges? Don't decide what it means. Just see where it is in its year, as precisely as you can. Hold that picture through the sit. The bell holds the time.
Seasons in the journal. Thoreau's habit of writing down when the ice broke and the plants flowered, year after year. Today's word.
Your line: keep records. Today, write down your plant's stage with today's date, and look at the same plant again next week. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Some people keep a seasonal record in Thoreau's spirit, noting the dates when one tree leafs out, flowers or turns color, which ties them to one place across the years.
